cultivar: Qimen Zhuye (local small-leaf population bush), with some newer local selections
processing: Fully oxidised: withered, rolled, oxidised in warm humid rooms and dried, then refined through repeated cutting, sieving, sorting and re-firing passes that leave the leaf short, slim and uniform.
harvest_season: Spring, mostly mid-April into May around Guyu; the first spring lots are the prized ones, summer leaf goes into the lower grades.
appearance_dry: Short, slim, tightly twisted strands, black with a faint grey-blue sheen and only a scattering of tips.
appearance_liquor: Bright red-orange and clear, with a golden rim where it meets the cup.
appearance_wet: Small, even, copper-red leaf pieces, soft and glossy.
taste_profile: Mellow and slightly winey, with cocoa, dried plum and the rose-like 'Qimen fragrance', a whisper of pine smoke in traditional lots, and a brisk but never harsh finish.

brewing.notes: Porcelain gaiwan, water around 90 °C; the cut leaf gives up colour fast, so keep the early steeps short. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes, no need for milk.

vintage_note: Sold by the current year's spring harvest; look for April lots picked around Guyu. It is at its best within a year to eighteen months of picking, after which the rose note fades and the cocoa flattens. It is not an ageing tea, and 'vintage' Keemun is a curiosity rather than a category.
description:
Keemun gongfu is the original Keemun: the refined, short-cut black tea from Qimen County in the hills of southern Anhui, made since the 1870s and the China black that gave old-fashioned English Breakfast blends their backbone. What sets it apart is the aroma the Chinese simply call 'Qimen fragrance' – rose and cocoa with a faintly winey edge – which comes from the local small-leaf Zhuye bushes and the cool, misty valleys they grow in, not from any flavouring.

The leaf is withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried like any black tea, and then the real 'gongfu' (effort) starts: the rough tea is cut, sieved, winnowed, sorted by size and re-fired in several passes, so what reaches you is a blend of tidy fractions rather than whole leaves. That is why the dry leaf looks so short and even, why the colour comes out of it so fast, and why it carries aroma so well in a blend.

Brewed properly it opens with cocoa and dried plum, moves into rose and honey in the middle steeps and finishes soft and malty. The classic mistake is treating it like an Assam: boiling water and a long steep pull out tannin and bury the fragrance. Use water around 90 °C and short infusions in a gaiwan, or 3 g per 250 ml for three minutes in a pot. It takes milk politely but does not need it.

Chinese grading runs from Li Cha at the top through Te Ming and Te Ji down to numbered grades; the higher the grade, the finer the cut, the more tips and the more aroma. Exporters often use their own labels (Hao Ya A and B for the top lots). Buy the current spring harvest and check that it actually says Qimen: a lot of 'Keemun' comes from neighbouring counties such as Dongzhi and Shitai, which can be good but is not the same tea. The whole-leaf styles (Mao Feng, Xiang Luo, Jin Zhen) are different products and should be sold under those names.

If you only know Keemun from a breakfast blend, a Te Ji grade brewed alone in a small pot is the quickest way to understand why people make a fuss about it.
sources_note: Grade ladder (Li Cha, Te Ming, Te Ji, numbered grades) is the traditional Qimen gongfu scheme; exact cut-offs vary by factory. 1870s origin date is the commonly cited one (often given as 1875).
